                    ### Question
                    A 29-year-old woman, obese, with no history of interest, who consulted for a bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache lasting one month, accompanied by horizontal diplopia and episodes of monocular amaurosis of seconds duration. The exploration is normal, except for the presence of bilateral papilledema. Which of these tests do you think will allow you to fully confirm your diagnosis ?:

                    ### Options
                    opa. Ultrasound of supra-aortic trunks.
opb. Magnetic resonance of the skull.
opc. Electroencephalogram.
opd. Lumbar puncture.
ope. Visual evoked potentials.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The presence of bilateral papilledema in this 29-year-old woman suggests increased intracranial pressure, which can be associated with serious underlying conditions such as tumors or other structural abnormalities. The symptoms of intense pulsatile headache, horizontal diplopia, and episodes of monocular amaurosis further support the need for imaging to identify potential causes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the skull is the most appropriate test as it provides detailed visualization of brain structures and can rule out lesions or abnormalities that may be causing the increased intracranial pressure. This aligns with the consensus that MRI is the preferred imaging modality in cases of suspected intracranial pathology. Other options, such as lumbar puncture or visual evoked potentials, may provide additional information but are not definitive for confirming the diagnosis in this context.
